Datadog's Q4 Guide Is Flat at $1.2 Billion: Sell the Slowdown, or Buy the Dip? ©@kanawatTH via Canva, @Sergey Shulgin from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Datadog grew third-quarter revenue 35% to $1.20 billion, then guided the fourth quarter roughly flat as its largest AI customer cut usage.

The guide assumes that customer drops to its contract minimum, and growth from everyone else is implied in the low to mid 30s.

Cloudflare grew 39% and guided higher, a sign the slowdown is confined to one Datadog account and not cloud spending broadly.

Datadog's first 2027 outlook, expected with fourth-quarter results in February, is the next real test.

Datadog (DDOG:NASDAQ) grew third-quarter revenue 35% to $1.20 billion, well above the top of its own range. Then it guided the fourth quarter to $1.19 billion to $1.20 billion, roughly flat with the quarter it just reported.

That flat line traces back to one account. Datadog's largest customer, an AI company it doesn't name, cut usage in the third quarter, and the guide assumes it falls to its contract minimum.

The shares sold off hard on the report. Yet one day later, Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) posted 39% revenue growth to $782.5 million, so cloud budgets don't look like they're shrinking across the board.

The real question is whether this is a one-customer problem or the start of something wider.

A beat with a flat finish

The third quarter cleared every bar Datadog set for itself:

Revenue of $1.20 billion, up 35% from $886 million, against guidance of $1.135 billion to $1.145 billion

Non-GAAP operating margin of 28%, up from 23% a year earlier

Free cash flow of $251 million, with $5.2 billion of cash and securities on hand

Customers paying $100,000 or more a year rose 20% to about 4,860. Datadog also lifted its full-year revenue outlook to $4.515 billion to $4.525 billion.

The problem is the shape of the next quarter. Here is the run the guide puts on pause…

Datadog (DDOG): total revenue, quarterly, $ millions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

A flat fourth quarter would mean growth of about 25% from a year earlier, down from 35%.

One account, one big drag

CFO David Obstler said the largest customer still spent above its minimum in the third quarter. So any usage above that floor would add revenue the guide doesn't count.

Strip that customer out, and fourth-quarter growth is implied in the low to mid 30s. Datadog also renewed several large accounts early, AI customers included, at bigger commitments but better volume pricing. That trims revenue in the short run.

CEO Olivier Pomel kept the longer pitch on AI. His team is building specialized models to help customers "move towards autonomous operations," he said in the earnings release. The first one, Scout 1.0, now powers its Bits Investigation tool.

title: Cloudflare Jumps 12% as Its “Even Higher Gear” Delivers the Fastest Growth in Nearly Four Years

Cloudflare Jumps 12% as Its “Even Higher Gear” Delivers the Fastest Growth in Nearly Four Years
Rexielyn Diaz

Trading disclosure
Cloudflare Jumps 12% as Its "Even Higher Gear" Delivers the Fastest Growth in Nearly Four Years ©@jittawit21 from jittawit21 via Canva; @3alexd from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cloudflare shares jumped 12% after third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, its fastest growth in nearly four years.

Akamai grew revenue just 6% in the same quarter, while Cloudflare raised its 2026 revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion.

Non-GAAP gross margin fell to 72.4% from 75.3% as AI traffic and developer workloads lean harder on the network.

The fourth-quarter report, expected in February 2027, will show whether management's promised GAAP profit arrives.

Cloudflare (NET:NYSE) shares jumped 12% on the morning of November 6 after its fastest revenue growth in nearly four years. Revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, and the company lifted its profit forecast for the third time this year.

The contrast with its oldest rival is hard to miss. Akamai Technologies (AKAM:NASDAQ) reported the same day, and its revenue grew just 6% to $1.122 billion.

"Our engine is firing on all cylinders, and we've found an even higher gear for this next phase of growth," CEO Matthew Prince said in the earnings release.

That higher gear has a cost, though. Gross margin keeps sliding as AI traffic and developer workloads lean harder on the network.

Growth sped up again

This was the third straight acceleration in 2026. Revenue grew 34% in the first quarter and 36% in the second before reaching 39%.

A few other numbers stood out:

Non-GAAP operating income rose 59.5% to $137.1 million, a 17.5% margin.

Adjusted EPS climbed to $0.38 from $0.27, against $0.34 expected.

Current remaining performance obligations grew 37%, so contracted revenue is keeping pace.

Guidance moved up as well. Cloudflare now expects 2026 revenue of $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion, up from $2.86 billion to $2.87 billion in August. Its adjusted EPS outlook rose to $1.35 from $1.25 to $1.26.

Here is how the top line has stacked up quarter by quarter…

Cloudflare (NET): total revenue, quarterly, $ millions, Q3 2024–Q3 2026 (TIKR)

A year ago, quarterly revenue was $562.0 million. That climb is the clearest sign the AI traffic story is turning into sales.

Developers and agents carry the load

Management credits the Workers developer platform and agentic workloads. Meanwhile, customers paying over $100,000 a year grew 25% to more than 5,000.

That mix explains why Cloudflare keeps pulling away from Akamai. Akamai's security revenue grew 9% to $622 million, and its cloud infrastructure unit grew 34% but brought in only $109 million.

Akamai gave up margin too. Its non-GAAP operating margin fell 6 points to 25%, so heavy infrastructure spending is pinching both companies.

So how far apart are the two on growth?

Investors interested in stocks from the Internet - Software sector have probably already heard of Paycom Software (PAYC) and Cloudflare (NET). But which of these two companies is the best option for those looking for undervalued stocks? Let's take a closer look.

There are plenty of strategies for discovering value stocks, but we have found that pairing a strong Zacks Rank with an impressive grade in the Value category of our Style Scores system produces the best returns. The Zacks Rank is a proven strategy that targets companies with positive earnings estimate revision trends, while our Style Scores work to grade companies based on specific traits.

This system places an emphasis on companies that have seen positive earnings estimate revisions, so investors should feel comfortable knowing that these stocks have improving earnings outlooks. But this is just one piece of the puzzle for value investors.

Value investors also try to analyze a wide range of traditional figures and metrics to help determine whether a company is undervalued at its current share price levels.

Our Value category highlights undervalued companies by looking at a variety of key metrics, including the popular P/E ratio, as well as the P/S ratio, earnings yield, cash flow per share, and a variety of other fundamentals that have been used by value investors for years.

PAYC currently has a forward P/E ratio of 19.33, while NET has a forward P/E of 248.83. We also note that PAYC has a PEG ratio of 1.01. This metric is used similarly to the famous P/E ratio, but the PEG ratio also takes into account the stock's expected earnings growth rate. NET currently has a PEG ratio of 6.12.

Another notable valuation metric for PAYC is its P/B ratio of 15.84. The P/B ratio pits a stock's market value against its book value, which is defined as total assets minus total liabilities. For comparison, NET has a P/B of 77.93.

Based on these metrics and many more, PAYC holds a Value grade of B, while NET has a Value grade of F.

Both PAYC and NET are impressive stocks with solid earnings outlooks, but based on these valuation figures, we feel that PAYC is the superior value option right now.

title: What Did Cloudflare Stock Investors Miss Before The Run?
detail:
What Did Cloudflare Stock Investors Miss Before The Run?
Trefis Team

Cloudflare (NET) stock rose 63.5% between May 13 and November 11, 2026, outpacing the 2.9% gain for the S&P 500. Sales growth accelerated during those months, and management credited its Workers Developer Platform and AI agent workloads across its network. The run appears surprising only if the AI demand behind Workers remained hidden until May. So when did AI demand for Workers first show up?

Cloudflare Tied Workers To AI In Early 2025

Management made this connection out loud on the call for the fourth quarter of 2024, held on February 6, 2025: "The killer application for Cloudflare Workers is turning out to be AI." On the same call, management said Workers could become the first choice for developers seeking the best price for performance. That statement arrived more than a year before the six months measured here.

On November 17, 2025, Cloudflare agreed to acquire Replicate, an AI platform that helps developers deploy and run AI models. So by late 2025, the company was putting money, not just words, behind AI for developers.

Did Cloudflare's Filed Quarters Show Faster Growth?

Yes, for three quarters in a row. Revenue growth against a year earlier rose from 26.5% in the quarter ended March 2025 to 33.6% in the quarter ended December 2025, and each quarter in between was faster than the one before. All of those quarters were filed before May 13, 2026.

The release for the December quarter, published on February 10, 2026, added a sign about new business. Cloudflare said it had closed its biggest contract ever by yearly value, averaging $42.5 million a year. The company also said new annual contract value grew nearly 50% from a year earlier. Then growth paused: revenue rose 33.5% in the quarter ended March 2026, roughly matching the pace of the quarter before.

What Had Changed At Cloudflare By November?

Growth had sped up again. Revenue rose 39.2% from a year earlier in the quarter ended September 2026. This pace came well above the March quarter's rate, and it represented growth across the entire company rather than a single product line. Peers did not move as one group during the same six months: Palo Alto Networks gained 46.8%, while Akamai Technologies fell 46.2%.

The 63.5% gain came after a fall. Every one of the signs from 2025 and early 2026 was public by May 13, and in the six months before that date Cloudflare stock fell 14.6%. So reading the signs early meant holding through that fall before the figures sped up again.

title: How Big Could Cloudflare Stock's Next Fall Be?

How Big Could Cloudflare Stock's Next Fall Be?
Trefis Team

Cloudflare (NET) stock lost 12.8% in the month to November 10, 2026, against 3.6% for the S&P 500, in a month when Akamai Technologies, Zscaler and Palo Alto Networks also fell. Buyers still pay 40 times the company's sales over the past year, betting that its growth keeps accelerating and its reported losses turn into profits. When markets sold off before, how much did Cloudflare stock give up, and for how long?

How Deep Did Cloudflare Stock Fall In Past Sell-Offs?

The 2022 inflation shock hit Cloudflare stock hardest: it fell 69%, while the S&P 500 fell 24%. Its largest fall at any time since its listing was deeper still: 82.6%, from its close on November 18, 2021, to its close on November 9, 2022. The market figures in this section are measured on the SPY fund, which tracks the index. Across the six market shocks the stock has traded through since its 2019 listing, it lost 30.7% on average, against 16.8% for the index. It fell further than the S&P 500 in all but one of them, the 2020 COVID-19 crash. The most recent, the 2025 tariff shock, took 40% off the stock against 19% off the index.

Cloudflare stock eventually returned to its pre-decline high every time. The median climb back from the low took 1.2 months, but recovering from the 2022 fall took 31.4 months, from its June 2022 low until January 2025. The stock closed lower still in November 2022 before that climb.

Cloudflare's Sales Are Growing Faster Than A Year Ago

Revenue rose 39.2% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026, against 30.7% growth in the same quarter of 2025, so the faster growth buyers are counting on has held so far. Management said the quarter's growth came in particular from its Workers Developer Platform, from AI agent workloads across its network and from its largest customers. Customers that management counts as large brought in 75% of revenue, up from 73% a year earlier.

Cloudflare Still Reports Losses, And Gross Margin Is Slipping

Based on the figures in its filings, Cloudflare still lost money in fiscal Q3 2026. Its operating loss was 7.3% of revenue, slightly wider than the 6.7% of revenue reported a year earlier. On management's adjusted measure, the operating margin reached 17.5%, the highest in the company's history.

Management expects Cloudflare to turn a GAAP profit in fiscal Q4 2026, arriving earlier than the 2028 deadline it set at its 2026 Investor Day. That profit remains a forecast.

Gross margin is lower than a year ago. Management said the adjusted measure fell to 72.4% in fiscal Q3 2026, down 290 basis points from a year earlier. That level remains inside the company's long-term target range of 70% to 77%. Management also said its Workers product has slightly lower gross margins than products such as Zero Trust, though it costs much less to sell.

title: Is It Worth Investing in Cloudflare (NET) Based on Wall Street's Bullish Views?

Is It Worth Investing in Cloudflare (NET) Based on Wall Street's Bullish Views?
Zacks Equity Research

NET

Trading disclosure

When deciding whether to buy, sell, or hold a stock, investors often rely on analyst recommendations. Media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm-employed (or sell-side) analysts often influence a stock's price, but are they really important?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Cloudflare (NET).

Cloudflare currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.56, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 32 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.56 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 32 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 23 are Strong Buy and two are Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 71.9% and 6.3% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for NET
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for NET

Check price target & stock forecast for Cloudflare here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Cloudflare, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Do you wonder why? As a result of the vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover, their analysts tend to rate it with a strong positive bias. According to our research, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations for every "Strong Sell" recommendation.

This means that the interests of these institutions are not always aligned with those of retail investors, giving little insight into the direction of a stock's future price movement. It would therefore be best to use this information to validate your own analysis or a tool that has proven to be highly effective at predicting stock price movements.

With an impressive externally audited track record, our proprietary stock rating tool, the Zacks Rank, which classifies stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), is a reliable indicator of a stock's near-term price performance. So, validating the Zacks Rank with ABR could go a long way in making a profitable investment decision.

Zacks Rank Should Not Be Confused With ABR

In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

The ABR is calculated solely based on brokerage recommendations and is typically displayed with decimals (example: 1.28). In contrast, the Zacks Rank is a quantitative model allowing investors to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.

title: Jim Cramer Calls Cloudflare “the Most Expensive Stock in the Market.” He Still Prefers It
detail:

NET
AKAM
OPAI.PVT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Jim Cramer Calls Cloudflare "the Most Expensive Stock in the Market." He Still Prefers It ©@da-kuk from Getty Images Signature via Canva
Key Takeaways

Jim Cramer told a Mad Money caller he likes Cloudflare more than Akamai, even though he called Cloudflare "the most expensive stock in the market."

Cloudflare trades at 169x forward earnings against 12x for Akamai, after growing 39% in the third quarter while Akamai grew 6%.

Cloudflare booked its first Act 4 revenue in the third quarter, including payments for helping OpenAI crawl more efficiently, but hasn't disclosed the amount.

On Monday's Mad Money, Jim Cramer took a call from a viewer who'd bought Akamai Technologies (AKAM:NASDAQ) at $103 and watched it slide to $78.

Cramer blamed the slide on a convertible bond sale ("they did this big convertible bond and everyone's running from it"). That same day, Akamai announced $2.2 billion of convertible notes, and the stock closed at $80.29.

Then he pivoted to Akamai's pricier rival, Cloudflare (NET:NYSE), and its CEO, Matthew Prince, whom he called "the real deal."

"I think that Cloudflare, even though it's the most expensive stock in the market, I like more than I like Akamai," he said.

Cramer's Right About Cloudflare's Price

Cloudflare trades at 169x its expected earnings over the next 12 months. Akamai trades at 12x, even after landing an $11.6 billion compute deal with Anthropic in September.

Most of that gap is growth. Cloudflare's third-quarter revenue rose 39% to $782.5 million, its fastest growth in nearly four years, while Akamai's rose 6% to $1.12 billion. And Cloudflare has been priced like this for years: 169x is close to its 173x average at quarter-ends since mid-2023.

Analysts Already Expect a Lot

Analysts expect Cloudflare's revenue to rise from $2.17 billion in 2025 to $5.09 billion in 2028, about 31% a year in both 2027 and 2028.

NET Revenue Estimates: 2023-2028 (TIKR)

That's full-year revenue, while management's goal is $5 billion in annualized revenue by the fourth quarter of 2028. A full year at $5.09 billion implies a fourth-quarter pace above that goal, so to justify 169x, Cloudflare has to beat estimates that already run ahead of its own target.

AI agents are the reason it might. Cloudflare said on its second-quarter call that non-human traffic passed human traffic on its network in May, and that if trends hold it could reach 1,000 times human traffic within five years.

Traffic only helps if someone pays for it. Cloudflare calls its effort to develop new internet business models Act 4, and Prince said the company recorded its first Act 4 revenue in the third quarter, including a service that helps OpenAI crawl more efficiently. It hasn't disclosed the amount. Carrying more traffic also costs money: GAAP gross margin fell to 71.2% in the third quarter from 74.0% a year earlier.
